sig-figs-calculator.quickAnswer: Type any number: leading zeros never count, zeros between non-zero digits always count, and trailing zeros count only if the number has a decimal point. The tool highlights exactly which digits are significant, shows scientific notation, and rounds your number to any count of sig figs.
keyFacts: All non-zero digits (1–9) are always significant.
Zeros between significant digits are significant: 20.03 has 4 sig figs.
Leading zeros are never significant: 0.00407 has 3 sig figs (4, 0, 7).
Trailing zeros count only with a decimal point: 4.700 has 4 sig figs, but 4700 has 2 (the zeros are ambiguous).
Exact counted numbers (12 eggs, 1000 mm in 1 m by definition) have effectively infinite sig figs.
Your result can never be more precise than your least precise measurement — that is why sig figs matter in science.
howTo: Type or paste any number, including decimals and scientific notation like 6.02e23.
Read the significant-figure count — significant digits are highlighted in color.
Set how many sig figs you want and read the rounded value below.
Use the scientific-notation line to see the number's order of magnitude.
If the input is not a valid number, the tool tells you instead of guessing.
For homework, count first with the tool, then do the rounding by hand to build the habit.
sig-figs-calculator.formula:
1. All non-zero digits are significant.
2. Zeros between significant digits are significant.
3. Leading zeros are never significant.
4. Trailing zeros are significant only if a decimal point is present.
Rounding: shift the decimal so N digits remain, round half up.
sig-figs-calculator.workedExample:
Input: 0.004070
Digits: 0 0 4 0 7 0 — leading zeros (first two) never count.
A decimal point is present, so the trailing zero counts.
Significant digits: 4, 0, 7, 0 → 4 sig figs.
Rounded to 3 sig figs: 0.00407 (the trailing zero drops).
Scientific notation: 4.0700 × 10^-3.
benefits: Settles every classroom argument about which zeros count — with visual proof.
Rounds correctly to any precision instead of eyeballing it.
Teaches the rules while it computes, not just the answer.
limitations: Follows standard school/lab rules: trailing zeros in numbers like 4700 are counted as not significant, though some contexts treat them as exact.
Rounding uses round-half-up on binary floating point — extreme 16+ digit inputs may show tiny floating-point artifacts.
Does not do sig-fig arithmetic (addition/subtraction vs multiplication rules differ) — it counts and rounds single numbers.
An educational tool: follow your course's or lab's specific conventions for graded work.

faqs.a: Leading zeros only set the decimal's position — 0.00407 and 4.07 × 10⁻³ carry the same information. They tell you the scale, not the precision.
By the standard rule it has 1 — trailing zeros without a decimal point are ambiguous. Write 1.00 × 10² if you mean 3, or 100. (with a decimal point) to show the zeros count.
Counted quantities (24 students) and defined conversions (100 cm = 1 m) are exact and have infinite sig figs — they never limit your result's precision.

faqs.q: How does rounding to N sig figs work?
faqs.a: The decimal shifts so that N digits stay left of the cut, the rest is rounded half-up, and the decimal shifts back. E.g. 0.004070 to 3 sig figs becomes 0.00407.
Yes — 6.02e23, 1.6E-19 and similar forms are accepted. Only the mantissa's digits are evaluated for sig figs.
Computers store decimals in binary, so very long inputs can show microscopic rounding artifacts. For normal school and lab numbers (under ~15 digits) results are exact.
